snippet.title: Why This Mars Battery Could Beat Lithium-Ion
snippet.description:
Most lithium-ion batteries tap out after a few hours. Take your personal data back with Incogni! Use code UNDECIDED at the link below and get 60% off an annual plan: http://incogni.com/undecided. This one just hit 100. And the tech behind it didn't start in a battery lab … it started on Mars, with a NASA experiment designed to split CO2 into carbon and oxygen. Here's how the system works and how it stacks up against lithium-ion for grid-scale energy storage. Could a battery born on Mars actually beat lithium-ion at grid-scale energy storage?

Watch Why America's Most Valuable Resource Is in Your Trash https://youtu.be/J3afhsZQuVM?list=PLnTSM-ORSgi7uzySCXq8VXhodHB5B5OiQ

Video script and citations:
https://undecided.tech/how-mars-technology-gave-us-cheap-energy-storage/

Corrections (clarifications):
Lot of confusion in the comments about how this actually works, so here's the short version. Think photosynthesis, not battery-in-a-tank.

Noon's system pulls CO2 from the air and splits it into solid carbon and oxygen using electricity. The oxygen vents back to the atmosphere; the carbon is what stores the energy ... it's the fuel sitting in the tank. To discharge, the carbon is reoxidized inside a solid oxide fuel cell, recombining with oxygen back into CO2 and releasing electricity as it goes. No net carbon released over a full cycle.

The Mars connection isn't a metaphor: Chris Graves, Noon's co-founder, helped build NASA's MOXIE. The box on Perseverance that made oxygen on Mars by splitting CO2. Same core chemistry, different job.

On "100 hours" — that's how long the system can keep delivering energy from a single charge, not a lifespan or degradation number. It's designed to fill the multi-day backup gap lithium-ion can't (the one we currently fill with natural gas peakers), not to replace lithium in EVs or hour-scale uses. Noon themselves say it's meant to complement lithium, not replace it.

What's still TBD publicly: round-trip efficiency is reported in the 60–80% range. Definitely lower than lithium's 85–95%, but in line with pumped hydro and the reason the LCOS math still works ($0.05/kWh vs $1.20/kWh for lithium at 100-hour duration). Real-world CapEx and cycle life will come from their 25 MW / 2.5 GWh pilot.

When the power goes out after a hurricane, snowstorm, flood, tornado, or any other disaster, the question is simple: will you be ready?

In this video, I show a simple DIY emergency backup power setup using an Eco-Worthy 12V 3000W inverter charger and a large 12V LiFePO4 battery bank.

The goal is not to build a complicated full solar system. The goal is to create a practical backup power solution that can help keep the essentials running when the grid is down.

This setup can be charged from a normal wall outlet before the storm hits, and it can also be expanded later with solar panels, a charge controller, or a generator.

For people who want backup power without the complexity of a full solar install, this is a great starting point.

⚡ WHAT THIS SYSTEM CAN HELP POWER

- Refrigerator
- Freezer
- CPAP machine
- Recliner
- Lights
- Internet router
- Phones and small electronics
- Small appliances
- Emergency essentials

This is not meant to power your whole house forever. It is a small emergency backup system designed to help you get through the critical first couple of days after a power outage.

🔋 WHAT YOU’LL LEARN

- DIY backup power for hurricanes and outages
- Eco-Worthy 12V 3000W inverter charger setup
- 280Ah and 300Ah LiFePO4 battery options
- Around 3.5 to 4kWh of battery storage

- When to move up to 24V or 48V
- How a generator can recharge the battery
- Why testing your real loads matters before an emergency

🌪️ WHY THIS MATTERS

If you live in hurricane country like Florida, or anywhere storms, floods, snow, tornadoes, or grid outages happen, having backup power ready before disaster strikes can make a huge difference.

A setup like this can be prepared ahead of time, charged before the storm, and used only when needed. It can also reduce generator runtime because the generator can recharge the battery instead of running all night.

That means less fuel use, less noise, and more flexibility during an outage.

- A 12V inverter charger

- Grid charging before an outage

It is simple enough for beginners to understand, but still powerful enough to run meaningful loads when the grid is down.

Can one inverter really work with both 24V and 48V battery systems?

In this video, I test the Junbpaw 2080W pure sine wave inverter with built-in ATS automatic transfer switch. What makes this inverter interesting is the 24V/48V auto-detect feature. Instead of being locked into one battery voltage, this unit is advertised as automatically detecting whether you connect a 24V or 48V battery bank.

That could be useful for DIY solar users who want to start with a 24V system and later move to 48V without replacing the inverter.

In this review, I go through the setup, battery connections, 24V testing, 48V testing, load testing, ATS transfer testing, and real-world thoughts on whether this is something I would trust in a DIY solar, RV, shed, backup power, or off-grid setup.

⚡ WHAT I TEST

* Junbpaw 2080W pure sine wave inverter
* 24V battery connection
* 48V battery connection
* Auto-detect behavior
* AC output testing
* Load testing
* Automatic transfer switch testing
* Bypass / shore power behavior
* Remote switch and display
* Wiring and battery cable setup
* Real-world inverter use cases
* What I like
* What concerns me
* Who this inverter might be good for

🔋 WHY 24V / 48V AUTO-DETECT MATTERS

A lot of DIY solar builders start small.

Maybe you begin with a 24V battery bank because it is cheaper and easier to build. Later, as your system grows, you may want to move to 48V for better efficiency, lower current, larger inverters, and longer wire runs.

Most inverters are locked to one battery voltage. A 24V inverter works on 24V. A 48V inverter works on 48V.

So if this inverter can truly handle both 24V and 48V automatically, that makes it a very interesting option for people who are still growing their system.

🧪 REAL-WORLD USE CASES

This type of inverter may make sense for:

* DIY solar projects
* RV power systems
* Solar sheds
* Small backup power systems
* Camping and mobile power
* Battery testing
* Emergency backup
* Systems that may upgrade from 24V to 48V later

But auto-detect does not remove the need for proper system design. You still need the right wire size, fuse size, breaker rating, battery capacity, grounding, and load testing before trusting any inverter in a real backup system.

⚠️ IMPORTANT TESTING NOTE

This is a review and test of the inverter, not a promise that it is right for every system.

Always size your inverter, batteries, wires, fuses, breakers, and loads correctly. DC power can be dangerous, especially at high current. If you are unsure, get help before wiring or testing an inverter.

A lot of DIY solar builders start small.

Maybe you begin with a 24V battery bank because it is cheaper and easier to build. Later, as your system grows, you may want to move to 48V for better efficiency, lower current, larger inverters, and longer wire runs.

Most inverters are locked to one battery voltage. A 24V inverter works on 24V. A 48V inverter works on 48V.
